# Multiple Regression

## Multiple Regression

So far, we've only examined the relationship between a continuous outcome and continuous predictor one at a time with *simple regression*. With *multiple regression*, we can examine these relationships **jointly**: looking at one relationship while adjusting for the relationships of other variables.

$$y_i = \beta_0 \, + \, \beta_1 x_{1i} \, + \, \beta_2 x_{2i} \, + \, ... \, + \, \beta_p x_{2i} \, + \, \epsilon$$

::: subpoint
○ $\beta_0$: value of $y$ when *all predictors* $x = 0$
:::

::: subpoint
○ $\beta_1$: slope of $x_{1i}$ adjusted for the effect of $x_{2i}, \, ..., \,x_{pi}$ 
:::


## Simple Regression

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
```{r}
library(palmerpenguins)

m1 <- lm(body_mass_g ~ bill_depth_mm, data = penguins) 
summary(m1)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Today's regression question: what is the effect of penguin bill depth on body mass?

::: fragment
The estimated penguin body mass when bill depth is zero is `r coef(m1)["(Intercept)"] |> round(2)`.

An increase in 1 mm in bill depth is associated with an `r coef(m1)["bill_depth_mm"] |> round(2)` g increase in body mass.
:::
:::
::::


## Standardizing

::: {style="font-size:80%"}
```{r}
penguins_cleaned <- penguins |>
  drop_na(body_mass_g, bill_depth_mm) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      ends_with("_mm"), 
      function(col) (col - mean(col)) / sd(col), 
      .names = "{.col}_z")
    )
penguins_cleaned
```
:::


## Simple Regression

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
m1 <- lm(body_mass_g ~ bill_depth_mm_z, 
         data = penguins_cleaned) 
summary(m1)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
The estimated penguin body mass for penguins with average bill depth is `r coef(m1)["(Intercept)"] |> round(2)`.

An increase in 1 SD in bill depth is associated with an `r coef(m1)["bill_depth_mm_z"] |> round(2)` g increase in body mass.
:::
::::


## Model Predictions

Once we've fitted the model, we can examine the model **predictions**.

:::: subpoint
○ What are the predicted outcome values for each datapoint in our dataset?

::: subsubpoint
○ Plugging in each observations' predictor values into the fitted regression equation.
:::

::::



:::: subpoint
○ What are the predicted outcome values new possible datapoints?

::: subsubpoint
○ Plugging in some possible predictor values for theoretical new datapoints.
:::

::: subsubpoint
○ Can be a helpful way of examining the model implications.
:::

::::



## Model Predictions

What are the predicted outcome values for each datapoint in our dataset?

::::::: {style="font-size:85%"}

:::::: {.columns}
::::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
```{r}
gtsummary::tbl_regression(m1, intercept = T)
```

$\widehat{\text{body mass}}_i = 4202 + -378 (\text{bill depth}_i)$
:::::

::::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
Now that we have estimated these regression coefficients, what if we plug back in each datapoints' predictor values to get predicted outcome values?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47.5%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
penguins_cleaned |>
  select(bill_depth_mm, 
         bill_depth_mm_z) |>
  head(2)
```
:::

::: {.column width="47.5%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
penguins_cleaned |>
  select(bill_depth_mm, bill_depth_mm_z) |>
  head(2)
```
:::
::::


:::::
::::::

::: fragment
`fitted.values()` and `predict()` will each extract these predicted values for you into a vector with a predicted value for each row in the dataset.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
fitted.values(m1) |>
  head()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
predict(m1) |>
  head()
```
:::
::::

:::

## Model Predictions

What are the predicted outcome values new possible datapoints?

::::: {style="font-size:85%"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
gtsummary::tbl_regression(m1, intercept = T)
```

$\widehat{\text{body mass}}_i = 4202 + -378 (\text{bill depth}_i)$

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Examining model predictions for theoretical new datapoints can be a way of exploring model implications.

With other predictors at their average ($x = 0$ because standardized), how does the predicted outcome change with increases in bill length?

::: fragment
```{r}
new_data <- tibble(
  bill_depth_mm_z = seq(-3, 3, by = 1)
)
new_data
```
:::

:::
::::

:::::


## Model Predictions

What are the predicted outcome values new possible datapoints?

::::: {style="font-size:85%"}

`predict()` will calculate predicted values on new possible datapoints for you into a vector with a predicted value for each row in the new dataset. Needs the `newdata` argument to be a `data.frame` or `tibble` with column names matching the predictor values.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
predictions <- predict(m1, newdata = new_data)
predictions
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
predicted_data <- tibble(
  bill_depth_mm_z = seq(-3, 3, by = 1)
) |>
  mutate(
    predicted_y = predict(
      m1, 
      newdata = tibble(bill_depth_mm_z))
  )
predicted_data
```
:::
::::

:::::

## Predictions with `ggpredict()`

The `ggpredict()` function from the `ggeffects` package can do this for us!

::::: {.columns}
:::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
No data by default...

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
# install.packages("ggeffects")
ggeffects::ggpredict(m1, terms = c("bill_depth_mm_z")) |>
  plot()
```

### Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
ggeffects::ggpredict(m1, terms = c("bill_depth_mm_z")) |>
  plot()
```
:::

::::

:::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
...but we can add!

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot

```{r}
#| echo: false

  geom_point(
    data = penguins_cleaned,
    aes(x = bill_depth_mm_z, y = body_mass_g)
  )
```

### Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
ggeffects::ggpredict(m1, terms = c("bill_depth_mm_z")) |>
  plot() +
  geom_point(
    data = penguins_cleaned,
    aes(x = bill_depth_mm_z, y = body_mass_g)

```
:::

## Confounders

One assumption of linear regression is that our model is correctly specifed.

::::: {.columns style="font-size:85%"}
:::: {.column .fragment width="70%"}
These results are an example of **omitted variable bias**. The relationship between bill depth and body mass *looks* negative, but we see clusters of *positive*-looking relationships.

[Since we have worked with this data so much, we know what the omitted variable likely influencing this clustering is:]{.fragment} [species!]{.fragment}

[Species as an omitted variable is currently **confounding** the relationship between bill depth and body mass.]{.fragment}
::::

:::: {.column width="30%"}
::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: "80%"
ggeffects::ggpredict(m1, terms = c("bill_depth_mm_z")) |>
  plot() +
  geom_point(
    data = penguins_cleaned,
    aes(x = bill_depth_mm_z, y = body_mass_g)
  )
```

### Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
ggeffects::ggpredict(m1, terms = c("bill_depth_mm_z")) |>
  plot() +
  geom_point(
    data = penguins_cleaned,
    aes(x = bill_depth_mm_z, y = body_mass_g)
  )
```
:::
::::
:::::

::: {style="font-size:85%"}
[We can account for species by including it as a predictor in our model, going from single to **multiple** regression!]{.fragment}

[Note that we may not have noticed this had we not looked at the predictions against the data.]{.fragment}
:::


## Multiple Regression

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
```{r}
m2 <- lm(body_mass_g ~ bill_depth_mm_z + species, 
         data = penguins_cleaned) 
summary(m2)
```
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
After adjusting for species, an increase in 1 SD in bill depth is associated with an `r coef(m2)["bill_depth_mm_z"] |> round(2)` g increase in body mass.

After adjusting for bill depth, the difference between Adelie and Gentoo penguins is associated with an `r coef(m2)["speciesGentoo"] |> round(2)` g increase in body mass.
:::
::::


## Predictions with `ggpredict()`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
```{r}
gtsummary::tbl_regression(m2, intercept = T) |>
  gtsummary::as_gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Bill Depth and Body Mass",
    subtitle = "Adjusted for species"
  ) 
```
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
ggeffects::ggpredict(m2, terms = c("bill_depth_mm_z", "species")) |>
  plot() +
  geom_point(
    data = penguins_cleaned,
    aes(x = bill_depth_mm_z, y = body_mass_g),
    inherit.aes = F
  )
```

### Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
ggeffects::ggpredict(m2, terms = c("bill_depth_mm_z", "species")) |>
  plot() +
  geom_point(
    data = penguins_cleaned,
    aes(x = bill_depth_mm_z, y = body_mass_g),
    inherit.aes = F
  )
```
:::
:::
::::



## Predictions with `ggpredict()`

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center
penguin_palette <- c(Adelie = "#FF8C00", Chinstrap = "#A034F0", Gentoo = "#159090")

ggeffects::ggpredict(m2, terms = c("bill_depth_mm_z", "species")) |>
  plot() +
  geom_point(
    data = penguins_cleaned,
    aes(x = bill_depth_mm_z, y = body_mass_g, color = species),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    shape = 21,
    alpha = 0.4,
    stroke = 1
  ) +
  scale_color_manual("Species", values = penguin_palette) +
  scale_fill_manual("Species", values = penguin_palette) +
  guides(
    x = guide_axis("Bill Depth (z)", cap = TRUE),
    y = guide_axis("Body Mass (g)", cap = TRUE),
    color = guide_legend(
      override.aes = list(
        alpha = 1,
        linetype = 0,
        fill = NA,
        shape = 21,
        size = 3,
        stroke = 1.2
      )
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Body Mass Predicted to Increase with Bill Depth",
    subtitle = "After adjusting for species"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = rel(1.7)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = rel(1.05), color = "grey35"),
    plot.title.position = "plot",

    axis.title = element_text(size = rel(1.05), face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = rel(0.95), color = "grey20"),

    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = rel(1))
  )
```

### Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
```

## Multiple Regression

::::: {.columns}
:::: {.column .fragment fragment-index=1 width="50%"}
```{r}
m3 <- lm(body_mass_g ~ bill_depth_mm_z + species + year, 
         data = penguins_cleaned) 
summary(m3)
```
::::

:::: {.column style="font-size:90%" width="50%"}
What if we add the year of measurement?

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
When species is Adelie and year is zero...? Intercept is negative?

:::

::::
:::::


## Adjusting Year

Let's let `year = 2007` be represented by zero, since that was the first year of the study.

::: {style="font-size:80%"}
```{r}
penguins_cleaned <- penguins |>
  drop_na(body_mass_g, bill_depth_mm) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      ends_with("_mm"), 
      function(col) (col - mean(col)) / sd(col), 
      .names = "{.col}_z"),
    year = year - 2007
    )
penguins_cleaned
```
:::


## Multiple Regression

::::: {.columns}
:::: {.column .fragment fragment-index=1 width="50%"}
```{r}
m3 <- lm(body_mass_g ~ bill_depth_mm_z + species + year, 
         data = penguins_cleaned) 
summary(m3)
```
::::

:::: {.column style="font-size:90%" width="50%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
In the first year of the study, the expected body mass for Adelie penguins was `r coef(m3)["(Intercept)"] |> round(2)` g.

In the first year of the study, the expected increase in body mass for Adelie penguins with 1 SD increase in bill depth was `r coef(m3)["bill_depth_mm_z"] |> round(2)` g.

In the first year of the study, after adjusting for bill depth, the difference between Adelie and Gentoo penguins is associated with an `r coef(m3)["speciesGentoo"] |> round(2)` g increase in body mass.
:::

::::
:::::


## Predictions with `ggpredict()`

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center
ggeffects::ggpredict(
  m3, 
  # first term is on the x, second term is color, third term is the faceting variable
  terms = c("bill_depth_mm_z", "species", "year")
) |>
  plot() 
```

### Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
ggeffects::ggpredict(
  m3, 
  # first term is on the x, second term is color, third term is the faceting variable
  terms = c("bill_depth_mm_z", "species", "year")
) |>
  plot() 
```
:::



## Predictions with `ggpredict()`

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center
penguin_palette <- c(Adelie = "#FF8C00", Chinstrap = "#A034F0", Gentoo = "#159090")

ggeffects::ggpredict(m3, terms = c("bill_depth_mm_z", "species", "year")) |>
  plot() +
  geom_point(
    data = penguins_cleaned |> mutate(facet = paste("year =", year)), # needs to match ggpredict's name
    aes(x = bill_depth_mm_z, y = body_mass_g, color = species),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    shape = 21,
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  scale_color_manual("Species", values = penguin_palette, aesthetics = c("color", "fill")) +
  guides(
    x = guide_axis("Bill Depth (z)", cap = TRUE),
    y = guide_axis("Body Mass (g)", cap = TRUE),
        color = guide_legend(
      override.aes = list(
        alpha = 1,
        linetype = 0,
        fill = NA,
        shape = 21,
        size = 3,
        stroke = 1.2
      )
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Body Mass Predicted to Increase with Bill Depth" |>
      str_wrap(80),

  ) +
```

# Regression Diagnostics

## Regression Diagnostics

With multiple regression, we want to check on...

- Normality of residuals

  + Relationships with other variables

- Multicollinearity among predictors

- Outliers


# Residuals

## Residuals

We want to see that our residuals are **normally distributed** and have constant variance across all levels of the predictors.

Can extract residuals from a model with `resid(lm_model)` or `residuals(lm_model)`.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
```{r}
residuals(m3) |>
  head(5)
```

:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-align: center
penguins_cleaned |>
  mutate(residuals = residuals(m3)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = residuals)) +
  geom_density() +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
If you had a model with only continuous predictors, you could `pivot_longer()` the columns with the predictor values (`names(coef(lm_model))`) so each predictor has a row: then you can just `facet_wrap()` by the predictor name!
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-align: center
m_numeric_only <- lm(body_mass_g ~ bill_length_mm_z + 
                       bill_depth_mm_z + flipper_length_mm_z, 
                     data = penguins_cleaned)

penguins_cleaned |>
  mutate(residuals = residuals(m_numeric_only)) |>
  pivot_longer(any_of(names(coef(m_numeric_only))),
               names_to = "predictor", values_to = "x") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = residuals)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth() +
  facet_wrap("predictor", scales = "free_x") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1)
```

# Multicollinearity

## Multicollinearity

Multicollinearity refers to the ability of *predictors* to be associated with *each other*.

High multicollinearity: when the predictors in the model can explain a high amount of variance in another predictor. 

![](../media/lab_13/multicollinearity_gossip.png)

::: footer
Image made with GPT-6 on 2026-11-12 (may or may not try to make my own to replace).
:::


## Multicollinearity

<div>
```{=html}
<iframe class="slide-deck" src="https://jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026/lecture/slides/27%20Regression%20Diagnostics/Lecture%2027%20Regression%20Diagnostics.html#/multicolinearity"></iframe>
```
</div>

::: footer
From Mark's [Lecture 27: More Regression and Diagnostics, Slide 14](https://jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026/lecture/slides/27%20Regression%20Diagnostics/Lecture%2027%20Regression%20Diagnostics.html#/multicolinearity) accessed on 2026-11-12
:::


## Consequences

I've simulated some data where two predictors (`x1` and `x2`) are correlated with different strengths: $r = (0, \, .33, \,, .66, \, .99)$. What happens as the multicollinearity increases?

[Inflated standard errors on partial regression coefficients]{.fragment}

::: panel-tabset

### Tables

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| layout-ncol: 4
#| fig-align: center
n <- 100
sim_dat <- tibble(
  pred_cor = c(0, 0.33, 0.66, 0.99)
) |>
  mutate(
    xs = map(
      pred_cor, 
      \(pred_cor) MASS::mvrnorm(
        n = n,
        mu = c(0, 0),
        Sigma = matrix(
          c(1, pred_cor, 
            pred_cor, 1), 
          nrow = 2, byrow = T)
      ) |> 
        as_tibble() |>
        set_names(c("x1", "x2")) |>
        mutate(y = rnorm(n, 4 * x1 + x2))
    ),
    res = map(
      xs, \(xs) lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = xs) |>
        broom::tidy(conf.int = T)
    )
  ) 

# sim_dat |>
#   select(pred_cor, res) |>
#   pmap(
#     \(pred_cor, res) res |>
#          mutate(p.value = gtsummary::style_pvalue(p.value)) |>
#         select(-c(statistic, conf.low, conf.high)) |>
#         gt() |>
#         fmt_number(columns = c(estimate, std.error), decimals = 2) |>
#         tab_header(glue::glue("Predictor correlation: {pred_cor}")) |>
#         cols_label(
#           term = "Term",
#           estimate = "Estimate",
#           std.error = "SE",
#           p.value = "p"
#         ) |>
#         tab_style(
#           style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
#           locations = cells_column_labels()
#         )
#     ) |>
#   print()


tables <- sim_dat |>
  select(pred_cor, res) |>
  pmap(
    \(pred_cor, res) res |>
      mutate(p.value = gtsummary::style_pvalue(p.value)) |>
      select(-c(statistic, conf.low, conf.high)) |>
      gt() |>
      fmt_number(columns = c(estimate, std.error), decimals = 2) |>
      tab_header(glue::glue("Predictor correlation: {pred_cor}")) |>
      cols_label(
        term = "Term",
        estimate = "Estimate",
        std.error = "SE",
        p.value = "p"
      ) |>
      tab_style(
        style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
        locations = cells_column_labels()
      ) |>
      tab_options(table.font.size = px(13)) |>  # 4 across is tight at the default 16px
      as_raw_html(inline_css = TRUE) |>
      htmltools::HTML()
  )

htmltools::div(
  style = "display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr); gap: 1em;",
  tables
)
```

## Superficial Check

In an example numeric-only model where bill depth, bill length, and flipper length are the predictors:

```{r}
penguins_cleaned |>
  select(bill_depth_mm_z, bill_length_mm_z, flipper_length_mm_z) |>
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
```


## Why Superficial? 

Suppose you have this dataset:

```{r}
#| echo: false
set.seed(1)

n <- 10000
d <- tibble(
  x1 = 5 + rnorm(n),
  x2 = 10 + rnorm(n),
  x3 = 2 * rnorm(n),
  x4 = 3 + 2 * rnorm(n),
  x5 = 4 + rnorm(n, 2),
  x6 = 8 + rnorm(n, x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5, 0.2),
  y = rnorm(n, x6)
) |>
  round(1)
```

```{r}
head(d)
```


And you fit this model:

```{r}
m <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6, data = d)
```


## Why Superficial?

::: {style="font-size:90%"}

If we just look at the bivariate correlations, we get this correlation matrix:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
d |>
  select(-y) |>
  cor() |> 
  round(2)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Not tooo bad, right?
:::
::::

::: fragment
Well, multicollinearity isn't just about the bivariate relationships of predictors, it's about the total amount of variance other predictors can explain in a predictor.
:::

::: fragment
What if we estimate a model of other predictors predicting `x6`?
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
```{r}
summary(lm(x6 ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5, data = d))$r.squared
```

:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
...that's a lot of explained variance.
:::
::::

:::


## Squared Multiple Correlations

For each predictor, we need to examine the *total amount of variance* that the remaining predictors can explain of it.

$$\text{body mass} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\text{bill length} + \beta_2\text{bill depth} + \beta_3\text{flipper length} + \epsilon$$

In the models

::: subpoint
○ $\text{bill length} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\text{bill depth} + \beta_2\text{flipper length} + \epsilon$
:::

::: subpoint
○ $\text{bill depth} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\text{bill length} + \beta_2\text{flipper length} + \epsilon$
:::

::: subpoint
○ $\text{flipper length} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\text{bill depth} + \beta_2\text{bill length} + \epsilon$
:::

what is the amount of variance the predictors (i.e., the *other predictors* in the model of interest)? 

We can assess the amount of variance predictors can account for in an outcome with $R^2$.


## Squared Multiple Correlations

The $R^2$ of these models (again, predictors in the model of interest trying to predict each other) is called *squared multiple correlations*, $\mathrm{SMC}$s. 

::: subpoint
○ $\text{bill length} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\text{bill depth} + \beta_2\text{flipper length} + \epsilon$
:::

::: subpoint
○ $\text{bill depth} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\text{bill length} + \beta_2\text{flipper length} + \epsilon$
:::

::: subpoint
○ $\text{flipper length} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\text{bill depth} + \beta_2\text{bill length} + \epsilon$
:::


## Squared Multiple Correlations

```{r}
multicoll_m1 <- lm(bill_length_mm ~ bill_depth_mm + flipper_length_mm, data = penguins)
summary(multicoll_m1)$r.squared

multicoll_m2 <- lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm + flipper_length_mm, data = penguins)
summary(multicoll_m2)$r.squared

multicoll_m3 <- lm(flipper_length_mm ~ bill_depth_mm + bill_length_mm, data = penguins)
summary(multicoll_m3)$r.squared
```


## Variance Inflation Factor

The presence of multicollinearity among predictors in the model increases the variance of the model estimates. We can examine this effect with Variance Inflation Factors ($\mathrm{VIF}$s).

$$\mathrm{VIF}_\mathrm{p} = \frac{1}{1 - \mathrm{SMC}_\mathrm{p}}$$

where $p$ is a given model predictor.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Our numeric-predictors-only penguin model:
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
car::vif(m_numeric_only)
```
:::
::::


Variance Inflation Factors indicate the factor by which the standard error has increased because of multicollinearity for that predictor.


## Tolerance

An alternative way of looking at this is with *tolerance*, which is just the inverse of $VIF$.

$$\mathrm{tolerance}_\mathrm{p} = \frac{1}{\mathrm{VIF}_\mathrm{p}} = 1 - \mathrm{SMC}_\mathrm{p}$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Our numeric-predictors-only penguin model:
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
1 / car::vif(m_numeric_only)
```
:::
::::

Tolerance indicates the proportion of variance in a given predictor that is independent of other predictors.


## Tolerance and $\mathrm{VIF}$

</div>

::: footer
From Mark's [Lecture 27: More Regression and Diagnostics, Slide 20](https://jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026/lecture/slides/27%20Regression%20Diagnostics/Lecture%2027%20Regression%20Diagnostics_v0.html#/vif-and-tolerance) accessed on 2026-11-20
:::


## Why Superficial?

Let's check back in with our other dataset:

```{r}
d |>
  select(-y) |>
  cor() |> 
  round(2)
```

:::: {.columns .fragment}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### VIF

```{r}
car::vif(m)
```


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Tolerance

```{r}
(1 / car::vif(m)) |> round(3)
```

:::
::::


## Original Example

:::: {.columns .fragment}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### VIF

```{r}
car::vif(m3)
```


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Tolerance

```{r}
(1 / car::vif(m3)) |> round(3)
```

:::
::::

::: fragment
Note that these say `GVIF`: this is the *Generalized* Variance Inflation Factor. It's *generalized* because some of the predictor models have categorical variables as their outcomes (penguin species).

No need to worry about the details of this---the column with `GVIF^(1/(2*Df))` can be interpreted the same as we are used to!
:::


# Outliers

## Outliers

Outliers are datapoints that fall far away from the rest of the datapoints.

::: subpoint
○ Might be an unusual predictor value (or unusual combination of predictor values)
:::

::: subpoint
○ Might be an unusual outcome value given the predictor values
:::

We can describe all datapoints based on their **leverage**, **distance**, and **influence**.

::: subpoint
○ High values on these characteristics may indicate a datapoint is an outlier.
:::


## Outlier Detection

:::: {.columns style="font-size:85%"}
::: {.column .fragment width="33%"}
### Leverage

Leverage represents the distance of a set of predictor values to the centroid of the predictor density

::: subpoint
○ Potential to affect regression results
:::

$h$, or "hat," values indicate how far a point is from the centroid
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="33%"}
### Distance

Distance values are unusual outcome values given the observations' predictors

::: subpoint
○ Based on an observation's *residual*
:::

Studentized residuals provide a measure of distance
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="33%"}
### Influence

Influence indicates the amount an observation actually changes the results of a regression.

Function of leverage and distance

Considers the difference in predictions if a datapoint were removed
:::
::::

:::: {.columns style="font-size:85%"}
::: {.column .fragment width="66%"}
Leverage and distance represent a potential to influence results, but don't necessarily mean the results were affected.
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="33%"}
Influence does represent the degree of change in the model!
:::
::::


## Leverage

Leverage represents the distance of a set of predictor values to the centroid of the predictor density.

One datapoint with very high X compared to others.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-align: center
set.seed(1)
n_people <- 100
d <- tibble(
  x = c(rnorm(n_people, 30, 4.5), 60),
  y = x + rnorm(n_people + 1, 0, 5)
)

d |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(10, 70)) +
  theme_classic() +
  guides(x = guide_axis(cap = T),
         y = guide_axis(cap = T))
```

## Leverage

Leverage represents the distance of a set of predictor values to the centroid of the predictor density.

One datapoint with very high X compared to others.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
A datapoint having high leverage is not about its relationship to Y. Here, the outlier falls comfortably in the regression line.

But you can see **why** datapoints with unusual X values have high leverage: moving or changing them slightly could drastically change the estimated "line of best fit."

:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-align: center
d |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(10, 70), ylim = c(10, 70)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(20, 40, 60, 80)) +
  theme_classic() +
  guides(x = guide_axis(cap = T),
         y = guide_axis(cap = T))
```


### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
```
```{r}
delta  <- 15                       # how far to move the outlier's Y up/down
out_id <- 101           # the high-leverage point

ver <- c("Outlier lower", "As observed", "Outlier higher")

# Three copies of the data, differing only in the outlier's Y
d_pert <- purrr::map2_dfr(c(-delta, 0, delta), ver, \(shift, v) {
  d |>
    mutate(y = if_else(row_number() == out_id, y + shift, y),
           version = v)
}) |>
  mutate(version = factor(version, levels = ver))

# Slope for each version, shown in the legend
slopes <- d_pert |>
  group_by(version) |>
  summarise(b = coef(lm(y ~ x))[2], .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(label = sprintf("%s  (slope = %.2f)", version, b))

lab <- setNames(slopes$label, slopes$version)
d_pert <- d_pert |> mutate(version = factor(version, levels = ver, labels = lab[ver]))
cols_fill <- setNames(c("#8FB8A8", "#7FA6C9", "#E8A07A"), lab[ver])
cols_line <- setNames(c("#5E8F7D", "#3F6E94", "#C2623A"), lab[ver])

# Pieces for the plot
rest    <- d[-out_id, ]
out_pts <- d_pert |> group_by(version) |> slice(out_id) |> ungroup()
out_obs <- out_pts |> filter(grepl("As observed", version))
arrows  <- out_pts |> filter(!grepl("As observed", version))

ggplot(d_pert, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  # the 'other' points, identical in every version
  geom_point(data = rest, aes(x = x, y = y), inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  # one regression line per version of the outlier
  geom_smooth(aes(color = version), method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              linewidth = 1) +
  # arrows showing the perturbation of the outlier's Y
  geom_segment(data = arrows,
               aes(x = out_obs$x, xend = x, y = out_obs$y, yend = y, color = version),
               inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "dashed",
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.09, "inches"), type = "closed")) +
  # the three versions of the outlier
  geom_point(data = out_pts, aes(fill = version, color = version),
             shape = 21, size = 3.5, stroke = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols_fill) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cols_line) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(10, 70), ylim = c(10, 80)) +
  guides(x = guide_axis(cap = TRUE), y = guide_axis(cap = TRUE),
         fill = guide_legend(title = NULL), color = guide_legend(title = NULL)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        legend.direction = "vertical",
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 11))
```

## Leverage

We can examine observations' leverage statistics with their $h$ "hat" values with `hatvalues(lm_model)`.

::: subpoint
○ Returns one hat value per observation (row), so we can attach the column to our dataframe
:::

Want to compare to a cutoff of $h > \frac{3(P + 1)}{N}$.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment width="33%"}
```{r}
hatvalues(m3) |>
  head(3)
```
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="66%"}
```{r}
penguins_cleaned |>
  mutate(hat = hatvalues(m3)) |>
  select(bill_depth_mm_z, species, year, hat) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(col) round(col, 3))) |>
  head()
```

:::
::::


## Leverage

We can examine observations' leverage statistics with their $h$ "hat" values with `hatvalues(lm_model)`.

::: subpoint
○ Returns one hat value per observation (row), so we can attach the column to our dataframe
:::

Want to compare to a cutoff of $h > \frac{3(P + 1)}{N}$.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
```{r}
n_predictors <- length(coef(m3)) - 1
n_observations <- nrow(penguins_cleaned)

cutoff <- 3 * (n_predictors + 1) / n_observations
n_predictors; n_observations
cutoff
```
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
```{r}
high_hats <- penguins_cleaned |>
  mutate(hat = hatvalues(m3)) |>
  filter(hat > cutoff)
  
high_hats |>
  select(bill_depth_mm_z, species, year, hat) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(col) round(col, 3)))
```

## Distance

Distance values are unusual outcome values given the observations' predictors

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Internally Studentized

$$ \frac{y - \hat{y}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{MS}_\mathrm{residual} \times (1 - h)}} $$

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Externally Studentized

$$ \frac{y - \hat{y}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{MS}_\mathrm{residual(i)} \times (1 - h)}} $$

**Recommended**
:::
::::


## Distance

We can examine observations' externally studentized residuals `rstudent(lm_model)`.

::: subpoint
○ Returns one studentized residual value per observation (row), so we can attach the column to our dataframe
:::

## Influence

Influence indicates the amount an observation actually changes the results of a regression.


## DFFITS

$$ \mathrm{DFFITS} =  \frac{\hat{y} - \hat{y}_{(i)}}{s_{\hat{y}_{(i)}}} $$

::: subpoint
○ $\hat{y}$: predicted value of $y_i$ when $i$ is included in the regression  
:::

::: subpoint
○ $\hat{y}_{(i)}$: predicted value of $y_i$ when $i$ is NOT included in the regression  
:::

::: subpoint
○ $s_{\hat{y}_{(i)}}$: standard error of $\hat{y}_{(i)}$
:::

How much would the regression line change if $i$ was not in the dataset?


## DFFITS

We can examine observations' DFFITS with `dffits(lm_model)`.

::: subpoint
○ Returns one DFFITS value per observation (row), so we can attach the column to our dataframe
:::

Want to compare to a cutoff of $\mathrm{DFFITS} > 1$ or $\mathrm{DFFITS} > 2 \sqrt{\frac{p \, + \, 1}{N}}$.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
dffits(m3) |>
  head(3)
```
:::

::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r}
penguins_cleaned |>
  mutate(dffits = dffits(m3)) |>
  select(bill_depth_mm_z, species, year, dffits) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(col) round(col, 3))) |>
  head()
```

:::
::::

```{r}
  ) +
```

```{r}
  guides(x = guide_axis(cap = T),
         y = guide_axis(cap = T))
```
:::


## DFBETAS

Similar to DFFITS, but examines change in estimated regression coefficients.

$$ \mathrm{DFBETAS} =  \frac{\hat{b} - \hat{b}_{(i)}}{s_{\hat{b}_{(i)}}} $$

::: subpoint
○ $\hat{b}$: predicted value of $b_i$ when $i$ is included in the regression  
:::

::: subpoint
○ $\hat{b}_{(i)}$: predicted value of $b_i$ when $i$ is NOT included in the regression  
:::

::: subpoint
○ $s_{\hat{b}_{(i)}}$: standard error of $\hat{b}_{(i)}$
:::

How much would the regression coefficients change if $i$ was not in the dataset?


## DFBETAS

We can examine observations' DFBETAS with `dfbetas(lm_model)`.

::: subpoint
○ Returns a **matrix** of DFBETAS values per observation (row), so we can still attach the column**s** to our dataframe with `bind_cols()`
:::

Want to compare to a cutoff of $\mathrm{DFBETAS} > 1$ or $\mathrm{DFBETAS} > \frac{2}{\sqrt{N}}$.

```{r}
dfbetas(m3) |>
  head() |>
  round(3)
```


## DFBETAS

We can examine observations' DFBETAS with `dfbetas(lm_model)`.

::: subpoint
○ Returns a **matrix** of DFBETAS values per observation (row), so we can still attach the column**s** to our dataframe with `bind_cols()`
:::

Want to compare to a cutoff of $\mathrm{DFBETAS} > 1$ or $\mathrm{DFBETAS} > \frac{2}{\sqrt{N}}$.

```{r}
m3_dfbetas <- m3 |>
  dfbetas() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  rename_with(\(colname) paste0("dfbeta_", colname))
m3_dfbetas |>
  head()
```

# Matrix Math in R

## Matrix Math in R

While most of the time, R functions will do the work of handling matrix math for us, it can be handy to know a few functions and operations to do matrix math yourself.

The `matrix()` function allows us to create matrices. We can also convert from a dataframe with `as.matrix()`.

`matrix(data, nrow = 1, col = 1, byrow = FALSE)`

By default, `matrix()` will input values down columns first. Change `byrow = TRUE` to swap to by rows first.

:::: {.columns style="font-size:90%"}
::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
c(1, 2, 3, 4) |>
  matrix()
```

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
c(1, 2, 3, 4) |>
  matrix(nrow = 2)

c(1, 2, 3, 4) |>
  matrix(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
```

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
M <- tibble(
  x1 = c(1, 2, 3),
  x2 = c(4, 5, 6),
  x3 = c(7, 8, 9)
) |>
  as.matrix()
M
```
:::
::::

## Transposing a Matrix

Transposition (denoted $\bf{M}^\top$ or $\bf{M}'$, read "M transposed" or "M prime") flips the matrix columns and rows. The `t(matrix)` function will transpose matrices.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
M
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
t(M)
```
:::
::::


## Matrix Multiplication

By default, using the `*` operator in R multiplies elements from each cell of a matrix.

```{r}
M * M
```

To apply real **matrix multiplication**, use the `%*%` operator.

```{r}
M %*% M
```

For vectors (single column matrices), this will compute the **dot product** and result in a scalar (one number).

```{r}
c(1, 2, 3) %*% c(1, 2, 3)
```


## Inverting a Matrix

A matrix multiplied by its inverse equals the identity matrices. In that way, it is similar to the **reciprocal** value for scalars.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Scalars

$$ x \times \frac{1}{x} = 1 $$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Matrices

$$ \bf{M} \times \bf{M}^{-1} = \bf{I} $$
:::
::::

To invert a matrix in R, use the `solve()` function.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
(M <- tibble(
  x1 = c(1, 0, 3),
  x2 = c(2, 3, 0),
  x3 = c(0, 4, 5)
) |>
  as.matrix())
```
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
solve(M)
```
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
M %*% solve(M) 
```

:::
::::
